claims.text: The baseline material is nanocrystalline W38Ta36Cr15V11.
W38Ta36Cr15V11 develops Cr–V-rich precipitates under irradiation near 8 dpa.
The Cr–V-rich precipitates cause or are associated with irradiation hardening.
The proposed intervention is addition of a few atomic percent Hf.
A minor Hf addition will suppress Cr–V-rich precipitate formation near 8 dpa.
A minor Hf addition will preserve the alloy's low hardening and radiation resistance.
Adding Hf will not create significant bulk-manufacturing challenges.
Hf enhances thermodynamic stabilization of the bcc solid solution by altering mixing enthalpy and chemical short-range order.
Thermodynamic stabilization of the bcc solid solution inhibits nucleation and growth of Cr–V precipitates.
Increasing the mixing enthalpy through Hf addition makes Cr and V less prone to segregation.
Hf may alter defect migration and recombination dynamics in the W–Ta–Cr–V alloy.
Altered defect migration can increase vacancy–interstitial recombination and improve radiation tolerance.
The unmodified W38Ta36Cr15V11 baseline has good radiation resistance, low hardening, and practical bulk manufacturability.
The Hf-modified alloy should have a lower precipitate density than the unmodified alloy at approximately 8 dpa.
Approximately 1050 K is representative of fusion first-wall or divertor service temperatures for this irradiation test.

contradictions.description: The baseline is described as having precipitate-induced or precipitate-associated increased hardening, while the central hypothesis and prediction characterize the property to be preserved as low hardening. These statements are not quantitatively reconciled.
